t: Alodia was the last of the three Nubian kingdoms to accept Christianity: in 580 the bishop Longinus baptized the king, his family and the nobility.
In the 10th century Ibn Hawqal and al-Aswani found a large, polyethnic kingdom more powerful than Makuria, with a capital of fine buildings and churches full of gold.
Succession was matrilineal, passing to the son of the king's sister, and al-Aswani wrote that the king could enslave any subject at will.
dyk: As late as 1930, Hamaj villagers in the southern Gezira would swear by 'Soba the home of my grandfathers and grandmothers which can make the stone float and the cotton ball sink'.
ev: John of Ephesus mentions Alodia for the first time, as a kingdom on the cusp of Christianization.
Longinus is sent at the king's request and baptizes him, his family and the nobility; Alodia joins the Coptic Patriarchate of Alexandria.
Makuria and the Arabs sign the Baqt after two failed invasions; the treaty explicitly leaves Alodia unaffected.
Al-Yaqubi describes Alodia as the stronger of the two Nubian kingdoms, a country three months' journey across.
Ibn Hawqal and al-Aswani visit the kingdom and describe Soba's prosperity under kings Eusebius and Stephanos.
The Damadim attack Nubia from the south, according to Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi; Soba may have been conquered and destroyed.
Al-Abwab, the northernmost province, is recorded as an independent splinter kingdom.
Soba lies in ruins; Abdallah Jammah and the Funj king Amara Dunqas destroy the kingdom, and the Funj found Sennar.

f.capital: Soba, near modern Khartoum at the confluence of the Blue and White Nile
f.predecessor: The Kingdom of Kush, which ceased to exist around 350, and the Nubian chiefdoms buried in the tumuli of El-Hobagi
f.successor: The Abdallab domain of Abdallah Jammah at Qerri and the Funj Sultanate of Sennar (1504–1505); by tradition, the Kingdom of Fazughli
